newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S. move seen boosting Russia share investment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. move seen boosting Russia share investment.

text.p: A U.S. nod of approval to Russian securities legislation could be a boon to equity investment in small companies and hasten the flow of funds pouring into the world's top-performing emerging market, analysts said on Friday.

Less than a dozen companies have seen the bulk of billions of dollars in new investment this year which has driven the Russian Trading System index of leading shares up about 150 percent in six months.
Russia was the best-performing emerging stock market in 1996, the International Finance Corporation has said.

Now the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, which keeps a close eye on mutual fund investment in emerging markets, has said Russian securities law meets many of the requirements for its approval.
The SEC indicated it would not block moves by mutual funds to drastically reduce the bureaucracy of Russian equity purchases.
"It will make it easier for the American players to come into the Russian market," said Yuri Kotler, spokesman for the Russian securities watchdog, the Federal Commission for the Securities Market.
"We have 30,000 companies and only 200 of them are really public and can trade and value their shares."

In a pincer action, the Federal Commission is also moving to consolidate the number of registrars in Russia, making more companies' shares accessible. "Make them bigger, control them tighter," Kotler said.
The Russian market is growing up and both moves have been on the wish list of conservative fund managers who have provided much of the market's new capital this year.
"The Russia letter (sent by the SEC in May to a U.S. law firm in Moscow) is proving the market has moved on," said CS First Boston's head of custody in Moscow, Nick Orchard.
"It is more or less evidence of the fact that the market has become more mature."
Lawyers for CS First Boston, which has about 700 companies registered, are drafting a short-form agreement, he said.

The SEC said it would take no action to force lengthy agreements to be signed between share registrars and Russian custodians, agreements necessary for mutual funds to buy shares, and the negotiation of which previously has taken months.
That should primarily be a boost for smaller companies with registrars which have not established relations with the major custodians -- shares which are coming on to investors' horizons.
"The market has shifted," said Bruce Lawrence, Head of international custody sales and marketing at UNEXIM Bank, one of Russia's major local custodians.

"A lot of investors are not looking at Russian Trading System One and Two (level shares) but at the third and fourth level. If a mutual fund wants those, the depositary will have to go out and negotiate an agreement."
But a wave of foreign funds will not fall at once on the unknown companies, which generally have only limited shares for sale, analysts say.
A Fleming Russia Securities Fund official said the primary obstacle to buying shares was liquidity rather than bureaucracy.
"The constraint to investment is finding stock," the official said.
Kotler said such improvements were the building blocks of investor confidence. "The more regulation, the more money can come in."
